title: A coding benchmark that fails a quarter of correct patches isn't measuring your model
summary: Two AI Engineer talks land on the same failure: coding benchmarks break at construction, with graders that measured about 8.5% false passes and roughly 24% false failures.
takeaways: Check your verifier in both directions before trusting any score: a grader that fails roughly a quarter of correct answers is measuring itself, not the model.
Read the actual prompts in a benchmark you rely on; audited coding tasks averaged around 481 words and some leaked the test file path or full interface.
Assume contamination by default and keep a private holdout set, because public benchmark prompts and answers turn up verbatim in model output.

sources.title: Nick Heiner (Surge AI): When Will The Benchmaxxing Plague End?
Ali Khial (G2i): Benchmarks — The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly

body:
## What happened

In a talk published 2026-08-02, [Nick Heiner of Surge AI](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-npY6XjM8CQ) argued that "benchmaxxing" — labs training too hard on benchmarks in a way that deviates from what people actually care about — persists because of incentives and poor methodology, not because benchmarks are useless. Most of his anti-patterns are construction failures, especially brittle verifiers (the code that decides whether an attempt passed): hard-coded string matches on phone-number formats that can't separate a weak model from a strong one, and IFEval prompts scored by checks that ignore whether the requested task was done at all — one response passes by substituting a Cyrillic character. Two days earlier, [Ali Khial of G2i](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jWq-aZIU0kM) put numbers on the same failure from his audit of coding benchmarks: citing DeepSWE comparison data, about 8.5% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks accepted wrong implementations and roughly 24% rejected correct ones, often because tests demanded unspecified variable names or probed unexported functions.

## Why it matters

A grader wrong in both directions injects more error than the gaps it is being used to measure. If roughly a quarter of correct patches are failed, a few points between two models sits inside the grader's own noise — and that is the number teams use to pick a model or gate a release.

## How it works

1. **Align the verifier two ways.** Heiner's prescription is verifiers aligned with the prompt in both directions, plus thorough QC — not just a check that rejects bad output.
2. **Read the prompts.** Khial found SWE-Bench Pro instructions averaging roughly 481 words, some leaking the test file path or a full interface — specs his engineers said no one would ever write.
3. **Keep a private holdout.** Both call for it; Heiner says contamination is the default, citing Opus reproducing SWE-bench Verified prompts and answers verbatim while model cards omit the disclosure.

> Before you trust a score, check the verifier both ways: does it fail wrong answers, and does it pass correct ones?

## The catch

Both talks come from inside the industry they audit — Heiner points to Surge's own Hemingway Bench — so read the prescriptions as interested advice. The 8.5%/24% figures come from one comparison on one benchmark, not a general law; rerun the check on your own eval. And Heiner's cost estimate explains why this keeps happening: 1,000 expert-authored agentic coding tasks pencils out near $15M, which he says is out of budget for most projects — an argument for paying for expert authorship on a small set rather than generating a big one.
